documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                BEFORE THE
                  FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


    Interconnection of Large Loads to the                      Docket No. RM26-4-000
    Interstate Transmission System



                          REPLY COMMENTS OF
               THE CALIFORNIA PUBLIC UTILITIES COMMISSION


        The California Public Utilities Commission and the People of the State of

California (“CPUC”) submit these Reply Comments in response to the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or “Commission”) October 27, 2025, Notice Inviting

Comments on the Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“ANOPR”) on large load

interconnection. 1

        The CPUC appreciates the opportunity to comment and express support for the

following issues identified in Initial Comments by industry and regulatory stakeholders.

Given the large volume of Initial Comments, the CPUC files these Reply Comments to

briefly highlight key issues raised for the Commission’s consideration. In its Initial

Comments, the CPUC raised that the proposed rulemaking, as described in the ANOPR,

extends beyond FERC’s jurisdictional authority. Many parties raised similar concerns,




1
  To distinguish load interconnection from generator interconnection, California refers to interconnection
of load as “energization.” Use of the term energization in these Reply Comments, unless otherwise
stated, is synonymous with “load interconnection.”


589841566                                           1
 and in these Reply Comments, the CPUC points the Commission to specific comments

that the CPUC believes helpfully explain the issues.

         If the Commission nonetheless moves forward, parties also raised helpful points

regarding the need for flexibility and deference to states within their domains and made

several proposals that would improve transparency in the large load energization process.

The CPUC adopts further positions on flexibility and transparency in response to these

comments, and supports methodologies proposed by other parties to effectively reach

those goals.

         Finally, given the broad range of megawatt (“MW”) thresholds for data centers

expressed by parties across the nation, the CPUC shifts its position toward a higher

threshold and supports considering non-MW factors to define the data center customer

class.

I.       JURISDICTION
         A.    The ANOPR is Inconsistent with FERC and Court Precedent
               and Proposes Jurisdiction in Excess of the Authority Under the
               Federal Power Act
         In its Initial Comments, the CPUC addressed why the proposed rulemaking, as

described in the ANOPR, would extend beyond FERC’s jurisdiction and undermine the

system of cooperative federalism set forth in the Federal Power Act and amendments in

the Energy Policy Act of 2005 (“FPA”). Many organizations, states, and industry

participants expressed similar jurisdictional concerns and advocated for the Commission

to adhere to the limits imposed by Congress on federal agencies. The CPUC agrees with

these entities and specifically identifies the following portions of Initial Comments that



589841566                                    2
 the CPUC believes clearly explain several of the jurisdictional issues raised by the

ANOPR.

          As discussed by the Organization of MISO States (“OMS”), the Commission’s

own analysis acknowledges the limits on its authority: “[t]he Commission recently

recognized the limits of its jurisdiction by rejecting Tri-State’s proposed High Impact

Load Agreement (‘HILA’). The Commission found that it would impermissibly intrude

on state-regulated retail rate matters by dictating specific terms and conditions of service

between utilities and their end-use customers.” 2

          And as explained by California investor-owned utility Pacific Gas and Electric

Company (“PG&E”), the ANOPR is misaligned with the Commission’s own precedent

on the balance between state and federal jurisdiction. PG&E’s “Rule 30” large load

energization application is before the CPUC. 3 PG&E notes the Commission determined

earlier this year that states have the authority to determine:

          1.     Which entities are legally permitted to provide electricity to retail
                 customers in co-location arrangements.
          2.     How the wholesale costs of providing electricity to those retail
                 customers are recovered through retail rates. That is true
                 irrespective of where the load interconnects (i.e., to the distribution
                 system, the transmission system, or the generator itself).
          3.     Their generation resource mix, including through their siting
                 authority (meaning co-located load is a question of state law). 4




2
    OMS Initial Comments at 5.
3
    CPUC Application No. 24-11-007.
4
    PG&E Opening Comments at 9.


589841566                                        3
          The ANOPR contradicts the Commission’s recent orders and claims jurisdiction

over transactions for electrons that never enter the interstate market. Under Commission

precedent, as quoted by PG&E:

         the Commission has exclusive authority over the rates, terms, and
         conditions for the sales from generating resources used to serve co-located
         loads, as well as the practices directly affecting such sales, provided that
         they are sales for resale in interstate commerce. If they are not sales for
         resale—that is, if they are made directly to the end-use consumer—or if
         they are not in interstate commerce then the co-located generator’s sales are
         under state jurisdiction. 5

         The CPUC agrees. The Commission and the states have separate zones of

exclusive jurisdiction. Critically, and key to the analysis here, the states retain authority

over matters not expressly granted to the Commission under the FPA. 6

         In its Initial Comments, the CPUC explained why the FPA does not provide FERC

jurisdiction over all things tangential to the transmission system or that have incidental

impact on wholesale electric rates. The Solar Energy Industry Association’s (“SEIA’s”)

helpful analysis of the FPA similarly demonstrated that Congress could not have intended

to bring within FERC’s jurisdiction any policy or action that may impact wholesale rates,

as “markets in just about everything—the whole economy, as it were” can influence

demand. 7 Instead, the U.S. Supreme Court has adopted a “common-sense construction of

the FPA's language, limiting FERC's ‘affecting’ jurisdiction to rules or practices that




5
    PG&E Opening Comments at 9-10.
6
    PG&E Opening Comments at 10.
7
 SEIA Comments at 7. (FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass'n, 577 U.S. 260, 277, 136 S. Ct. 760, 774, 193
L. Ed. 2d 661 (2016), as revised (Jan. 28, 2016).)


589841566                                        4
 ‘directly affect the [wholesale] rate.’” 8 Applying that analysis to the present large load

energization issue, retail loads are not direct participants in wholesale markets. 9 Rather,

they are retail end-use customers whose operations may indirectly influence wholesale

prices by contributing to demand. 10

           This type of indirect impact is beyond the scope of the Commission’s jurisdiction

under the Federal Power Act. 11 Further still, even if the proposals in this ANOPR do not

directly impinge on the states’ authority over retail sales of electricity, that does not itself

establish federal authority – “the Commission must clearly articulate how exercising

jurisdiction over large load interconnections is consistent with, but not derivative of, its

authority over wholesale transactions and transmission in interstate commerce.” 12

           The National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (“NARUC”) and

Edison Electric Institute (“EEI”) comments raised another jurisdictional concern. As

NARUC pointed out in its comments, FPA section 212(h) prohibits FERC from directing

the provision of transmission directly to end users (retail wheeling). 13 The FPA

reservation of jurisdiction over retail rates and services to the states includes retail load

energization. 14 Similarly, EEI comments analyzed FPA section 212(h) and demonstrated




8
    Id.
9
    SEIA Comments at 7.
10
     Id.
11
     Id.
12
     Id.
13
     NARUC Initial Comments at 4.
14
     Id.


589841566                                       5
 Congress prohibited the Commission “from ordering retail transmission service against

the wishes of a state, if the state prohibits wheeling to an ultimate consumer.” 15 The

Commission in Order No. 888 recognized this as a barrier to ordering a retail customer to

take service under a FERC-jurisdictional tariff. 16

            As NARUC’s comments explained, state commissions are the venue for retail end-

use customers to redress their rights when directly affected by the services of the electric

supplier. 17 State jurisdiction over retail load allows those customers to seek recourse

from state regulators’ decisions by participating in state proceedings and through electing

or influencing the appointment of state regulators. 18 The CPUC strongly agrees with

NARUC that the federal government and the states working together under the tradition

of cooperative federalism will lead to the most optimal solutions. 19

            In its comments, EEI also explained the critical point that the state regulatory

authority over retail sales is a power recognized by the same statutory provision that

authorizes the Commission’s transmission jurisdiction. 20 16 U.S.C. § 824(b) gives the

Commission jurisdiction over “transmission of electric energy,” but recognizes state

jurisdiction over “any ... sale of electric energy” other than “sale of electric energy at




15
     EEI Comments at 27-28.
16
     Id.
17
     Id. at 6.
18
     Id. at 6.
19
     Id.
20
     EEI Comments at 26.


589841566                                         6
 wholesale.” The terms of large load energization are not a sale of electric energy at

wholesale and therefore fall into the “any other” category reserved for the states.

           Further, EEI correctly raised that in Order 888, the Commission found that in all

cases, retail service involves state jurisdiction even if no distribution facility is actually

used. 21 The Commission concluded that requiring the unbundling of retail transmission

and generation would raise “difficult jurisdictional issues.” 22 A federal order claiming

jurisdiction over all retail transmission would have even greater implications for the

states’ regulation of retail sales. 23 Thus, even if a retail large load customer connects

directly to the transmission system, Commission precedent dictates that interconnection

to a distribution facility is not required for a transaction to be retail service under state

jurisdiction. 24

           B.      A Shift in Jurisdiction Would Leave Regulatory Gaps and Cause
                   Delays
           In its Initial Comments, the CPUC focused on the legal issues with jurisdiction

that may be invoked in this rulemaking. In these Reply Comments, the CPUC joins

others in the practical concerns and unintended downstream impacts of a jurisdictional

shift.

           Many parties helpfully noted the unintended consequences of hashing out issues of

jurisdiction at a time when speed is the goal. As explained by the Organization of PJM


21
     EEI Comments at 26.
22
     Id.
23
     Id.
24
     Id.


589841566                                       7
 States, Inc. (“OPSI”), “…expansion in Federal jurisdiction would lead to confusion and

likely conflict between federal regulation and state-approved tariffs.” 25 Research of

electrical utilities has found that, consistent with other industries, “perceived regulatory

instability reduces new investment and undermines policy goals.”26

          As further pointed out by OMS, the ANOPR presents a slippery slope that could

cause a massive shift from established operations and force retail unbundling. This

would cause further uncertainty and delay, as related processes would need to be

reconsidered to address resulting jurisdictional and operational changes, gaps, and

misalignment of regulatory authority. To quote OMS:

          FERC has consistently recognized, including in Order Nos. 2003 and 2023,
          that interconnection service is distinct from transmission service. Yet
          under the ANOPR’s reasoning, the act of connecting a large retail customer
          directly to transmission facilities could transform that retail delivery into a
          FERC-jurisdictional wholesale transaction – redefining distribution
          facilities and costs as transmission assets, shifting oversight of distribution
          expansion, maintenance, and rate recovery from state commissions to
          FERC.

          The ANOPR states that is not the intent; however, if it occurs functionally,
          many related processes (and regulatory constructs or arrangements) would
          need to be reconsidered to address resulting jurisdictional and operational
          changes, gaps, and misalignment of regulatory authority. If this
          reclassification of large load occurs, it will effectively compel states to
          unbundle retail service – a massive structural change with significant
          implications for ratepayers. 27




25
     OPSI Initial Comments at 9-10.
26
  “The Effect of Regulatory Uncertainty on Investment: Evidence from Renewable Energy Generation,”
Kira R. Fabrizio, Journal of Law, Economics, & Organization, Vol. 29, No. 4 (August 2013), at 765-798.
https://www.jstor.org/stable/23487259
27
     OMS Initial Comments at 7.


589841566                                         8
 OMS further outlined the impacts of such a jurisdictional shift:
          1.     existing customers would not be able to benefit from
                 spreading a utility’s generation and distribution fixed costs
                 over additional sales if large loads are not subject to an
                 incumbent utility’s retail tariff provisions;
          2.     the cost to procure sufficient capacity to serve the new
                 system load would likely be socialized and may increase
                 the potential for stranded costs if load does not materialize
                 as expected;
          3.     transmission congestion patterns may shift abruptly and
                 significantly, depending on the size of the large load,
                 thereby creating new network topology challenges and
                 increased congestion costs;
          4.     existing customers could experience increased
                 transmission costs through additional reliability projects;
                 and
          5.     any reliance on the grid for backup energy would increase
                 the need for system capacity, energy, and ancillary services
                 resulting in additional downstream costs for retail
                 ratepayers. 28
          Finally, as OMS pointed out, impingement on states’ jurisdictional authority may

create a regulatory gap where no entity is accountable for reliability or determination of

prudence.

          The Commission should include clear provisions ensuring that this
          interconnection process does not circumvent state-jurisdictional cost
          recovery mechanisms or retail service obligations. If the Commission were
          to override or bypass these structures, it would effectively separate
          interconnection from service responsibility, creating a regulatory gap where
          no entity is clearly accountable for maintaining reliability or ensuring costs
          are prudently assigned or recovered. 29




28
     OMS Initial Comments at 8.
29
     OMS Initial Comments at 12.


589841566                                       9
          The National Conference of State Legislatures (“NCSL”) also effectively

highlighted the uncertainty of responsibility by raising the following questions:

         1.     Who bears responsibility for managing and mitigating the ensuing
                reliability concerns?
         2.     Who is responsible for bearing the costs of increased power
                demand?
         3.     Which entity holds operational authority for determining customer
                prioritization during system restoration efforts? 30
         The ANOPR raises these and many other questions that the Commission would

need sufficient time to address. Therefore, either this process would slow energization of

large load and extend the timeline for bringing AI data centers online, or these questions

would go unaddressed, resulting in unreasonable cost-shifting and a less reliable electric

grid for all.

         C.     Sufficient Time is Necessary to Address an Issue of this
                Importance
         As explained above, the CPUC and many others have raised significant

jurisdictional concerns with the proposed rulemaking. But if it is to move forward, it is

of significant interest across the nation and should not be rushed toward final action by

April 2026. Instead, this ANOPR should be used to refine the proposals and prompts for

a subsequent Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (“NOPR”), providing sufficient time for

input from utilities, grid operators, customers, and other stakeholder groups.

         The Commission is required to “consider and take final action on any proposal

made by the Secretary . . . in an expeditious manner in accordance with such reasonable



30
     NCSL Comments at 2.


589841566                                    10
 time limits as may be set by the Secretary for the completion of action by the

Commission on any such proposal.” 31 To echo PJM Transmission Owners’ Opening

Comments, a “reasonable” time “must allow for the required rulemaking procedures set

forth in the APA, including a sufficiently specific NOPR and opportunity for meaningful

comment. …[A]n ANOPR is a precursor to the rulemaking process further support that

any forthcoming rulemaking must adhere to typical rulemaking requirements.” 32 The

time limit set in this FERC Docket is inconsistent with the full rulemaking process and is

not “reasonable” within the meaning of 42 U.S.C. § 7173(b).

          Large load energization is an issue of significant nationwide importance, and

while the CPUC is aligned on the goal of timely energization, sufficient time is needed to

develop transparent, effective, and durable rules. As pointed out by EEI, “[i]n any

Commission rulemaking effort, the amount of time needed for transition and

implementation processes necessarily depends on the nature of the Final Rule. The

Commission should ensure an appropriate transition period to implement any new rule.

We can only provide realistic implementation feedback in response to a NOPR rather

than an abbreviated ANOPR.” 33

          Further, the National Association of Utility Consumer Advocates (“NASUCA”)

asserts, and the CPUC agrees, that the Principles for Reform expressed in the ANOPR are

not actual reforms, but are the principles that actual reforms could incorporate.


31
     42 U.S.C. § 7173(b) (emphasis added).
32
     PJM TO Comments at 38-40.
33
     EEI Comments at 36-37.


589841566                                     11
 NASUCA also notes that a number of the principles create confusion with inconsistent

language and ambiguities. For these reasons, NASUCA concludes that more time is

needed in this docket. “Given the magnitude of the request and the importance of the

issues implicated by that request, it would be patently unreasonable and bad public policy

for FERC to use an expedited process to expand its jurisdiction.” 34

II.       FLEXIBILITY
          At the outset, the CPUC does not agree that the FPA has granted the Commission

regulatory authority to set rules over the terms and conditions of retail load energization.

However, should the Commission nonetheless move forward with making such rules, a

flexible application of any rule would likely be most effective. The CPUC echoes

parties’ comments that flexibility and deference to states within their domains would

benefit ratepayers, utilities, and industry alike. Otherwise, the ANOPR’s efforts may be

counterproductive to the mutual goal of promptly energizing AI data centers. 35

          A.     Stability Benefits Markets and Investment in Infrastructure
          Large economic investments needed for our electric grid and AI development

goals are best served by stability of investors’ expectations and reliability of economic

returns. Regulatory stability is one critical element of creating fertile conditions for

large-scale investment.

            Same as EEI, the CPUC wishes to “underscore the importance of providing a

clear signal to market participants that the progress they have made to bring large load


34
     NASUCA Initial Comments at 10-11.
35
     EEI Comments at 22.


589841566                                     12
 customers onto the system will not be undermined. Across the country, there are

countless large load customers who are already interconnected to the transmission system

or are in various stages of working through the process to interconnect.” 36 This ANOPR

comes at a time when many utilities, states, and industry customers have already

established processes and expectations for large load energization.

           B.     Less Intervention Will Lead to More Progress
           The CPUC also agrees with EEI that some of the ANOPR’s efforts may be

counterproductive to the mutual goal of promptly energizing AI data centers. 37 Like EEI,

the CPUC supports the goal of the Administration, Department of Energy, and the

Commission to advance the fair and rapid energization of large loads. 38 However, these

goals can best be achieved without reshuffling the deck and “calling into question the

way in which states and the Commission have traditionally regulated bundled retail

service and without launching a cumbersome new regulatory effort that is likely to slow,

not speed, progress.” 39

           If the proposed rulemaking takes the shape of a sweeping one-size fits all solution,

it will counterproductive. As well-stated by Duke Energy (“Duke”):

           To the extent FERC can identify specific and concrete problems within its
           statutory authority, FERC should narrowly tailor any proposed reforms to
           solving those specific problems. To attempt through this rulemaking
           proceeding to solve for theoretical problems, edge case hypotheticals, or
           problems beyond FERC’s statutory purview will introduce a quagmire of

36
     EEI Comments at 4.
37
     EEI Comments at 22.
38
     Id.
39
     Id.


589841566                                       13
            jurisdictional issues and disputes, thorny implementation details,
           unintended consequences, and lengthy, litigious compliance processes that
           would impede more timely interconnection of large load customers. Any
           reforms that FERC pursues must be catalysts, not quicksand. 40

           C.    Cooperative Federalism
           The CPUC joins other parties in encouraging the Commission to build on the

progress and experience that has already been developed by the states in energizing large

load and data centers currently serving the country.

           The CPUC agrees with the cooperative federalism approach proposed by OMS of

“developing voluntary best practices with states to improve interconnection efficiency,

requiring load interconnection processes that enhance transparency, and other novel

approaches” necessary at a particular moment. 41 This would dovetail with and preserve

state authority and established regulatory frameworks on state-jurisdictional issues that

ensure reliability, resource adequacy, and affordability. 42

           D.    Guidelines Instead of Fixed Rules
           Given state and regional differences and quickly evolving technology and markets,

flexible guidelines would be more effective than cumbersome rules.

           The CPUC shares EEI’s urging to the Commission to avoid being overly

prescriptive and to preserve contracting flexibility. 43 As EEI stated, “[l]arge load

customers are not uniform; their load characteristics may vary widely depending on the


40
     Duke Comments at 2.
41
     OMS Initial Comments at 8.
42
     Id.
43
     EEI Comments at 20.


589841566                                      14
 end-use and evolve over time.” 44 Guidelines establishing the type of technical

information large load customers need to provide prior to initiating an energization

request will improve infrastructure planning. 45

           The CPUC also agrees, as pointed out by Meta, that overspecification would be

counterproductive: “Issuing a detailed, standard rule that fails to account for the diversity

in the economic landscape could slow down successful interconnection processes and

undermine the Commission’s goal of bringing more data centers online faster and in a

more orderly manner.” 46

           Similarly, as stated by EEI, large load energization is a changing landscape: “Any

standardized procedures dealing with large load interconnection, including any efforts to

address the costs of studying these customers, must be flexible enough to account for the

evolving understanding of just what is necessary to integrate these customers to the

grid.” 47 The State of California Department of Water Resources (“DWR”) encouraged

that the Final Rule “adopt principles that guide the RTOs in their treatment of large load

interconnections—but each RTO should be given the latitude to adopt a program that

works best for its region.” 48 The CPUC agrees.




44
     Id.
45
     Id.
46
     Meta Comments at 3.
47
     EEI Comments at 21.
48
     DWR Comments at 9.


589841566                                      15
            Finally, quoting the California Independent System Operator (“CAISO”),

flexibility is best for reaching our mutual goals: 49

           Having the flexibility to align any large load processes with reforms
           already accepted and implemented by transmission providers in close
           coordination with their State policymakers will further the goals of the
           ANOPR. Large load interconnection studies may require specific
           mechanisms for transmission owners experienced in conducting such
           studies, as well as mechanisms to avoid the State-jurisdictional concerns
           that led to the Commission’s rejecting the rules proposed in Tri-State. This
           flexibility will facilitate a faster compliance process to help large loads
           interconnect as soon as possible and with greater regulatory certainty. 50
III.       TRANSPARENCY
           Again, the CPUC does not agree that the FPA has granted the Commission

regulatory authority over the terms and conditions of retail load energization. However,

should the Commission move forward with making such rules, the CPUC echoes and

supports a number of proposals from the Initial Comments, such as public posting of

interconnection requests and cost responsibility determinations, that would improve

transparency in the large load energization process. Transparency would benefit the

development and fairness of load energization, to the benefit of businesses and ratepayers

alike. The CPUC flags the following transparency issues relevant to large load

energization: (A) queue transparency, (B) access for Tribal governments through process

and capacity support, (C) data for load and capacity forecasting, (D) clarity of

methodology for cost causation and allocation, and (E) standard definition of parameters

that serve as inputs to said methodology (e.g., the definition of a “network upgrade”).



49
     CAISO Initial Comments at 8.
50
     Id.


589841566                                       16
            A.     Queue Transparency
           Queue transparency is necessary to reduce regulatory burden, ease energization,

and ensure system reliability. The CPUC supports implementing safeguards as

articulated by OMS, to prevent “load shopping” among transmission providers and

“queue gaming” by large-load customers with significant financial resources. 51

           Queue transparency measures will help create accountability and prudent system

planning. As put forward by the Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel (“OCC”),

transparency measures “are necessary to protect residential consumers from bearing the

costs of overbuilt transmission infrastructure resulting from inaccurate or inflated demand

projections.” 52 Reporting requirements should include reporting of queue attrition rates

and coordination with state regulators on load forecasting will further promote

accountability and prudent system planning. 53 Queue transparency would avoid

duplicative load requests from being used to develop utility load forecasts, which then

inform wholesale rates and transmission planning, and would improve the accuracy of

these processes. 54

           The CPUC also agrees with LS Power’s proposal that large load energization

information should be published, similarly to generation interconnection queue

information. 55 The CPUC supports the several concrete requirements to bring about



51
     OMS Initial Comments at 12.
52
     OCC Comments at 8.
53
     Id.
54
     SEIA Initial Comments at 3.
55
     LS Power Initial Comments at 6-7.


589841566                                      17
 queue transparency suggested by the OCC. The CPUC agrees with OCC’s proposal that

the Commission should require public utilities, Regional Transmission Organizations and

Independent System Operators to provide public posting of:

          1.      All interconnection requests above [the MW threshold], including
                  project type and location;
          2.      Cost responsibility determinations and any resulting upgrades; and
          3.      Annual reporting on the consumer cost impacts of large-load
                  interconnections, associated transmission expansions, and the impact
                  on electricity and capacity markets rates for consumers other than
                  large loads. 56
          B.      Access for Tribal Governments
          The CPUC supports Tribal Nations’ requests for robust process inclusion and

capacity support to enable full participation of impacted parties in both the rulemaking

process and any large load energization process(es) it produces. To quote the Chairman

of the Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakima Nation, “Meaningful Consultation

requires that we receive timely access to draft rule language, relevant data, and

implementation plans, and that FERC provide adequate technical assistance and capacity

support to enable full participation.” 57 As stated by Alliance for Tribal Clean Energy,

“[c]onsultation must occur before any approval of large load interconnections, include

data transparency and cost-allocation safeguards, and provide mechanisms for Tribal

review and mitigation of infrastructure impacts.” 58




56
     OCC Comments at 3-4.
57
     Yakima Nation Initial Comments at 2.
58
     Alliance for Tribal Clean Energy Initial Comments at 4.


589841566                                            18
            C.     Data for Load and Capacity Forecasting
           The CPUC also agrees with the Industrial Customer Organizations that data

reporting would be useful for both a grid operator and industry perspective. Quoting

Industrial Customer Organizations, “[a]ccurate, transparent forecasting provides two

critical benefits: it facilitates creative industry solutions and promotes accountability,

both of which lead to a more efficient grid. … the Commission should consider

developing rules that strengthen regional grid operators’ ability to develop accurate and

transparent forecasts. Providing transparency to industry stakeholders promotes an

increase of innovative solutions and better regional transmission and resource adequacy

planning.” 59

           Each utility uses its own methods and assumptions for developing forecasts, and

uniformity would improve accuracy. 60 EIA stated that “establishing transparent

forecasting assumptions and requiring standardized reporting by load-serving entities

would improve the accuracy of the load forecasts that feed into transmission planning and

market operations.” 61 The CPUC supports robust reporting requirements, provided there

is flexibility for regional variation and the ability to expand what data is gathered, and has

taken steps to implement them under our own jurisdiction.




59
     Industrial Customer Orgs Joint Comments at 27.
60
     Id.
61
     Id.


589841566                                             19
         D.     Clarity of Methodology for Cost Causation and Allocation
        Transparency in methodology for cost causation and cost allocation is critical to

ensure the costs related to large load customers transmission network upgrades

(“TNU’s”) are not unreasonably allocated in electricity rates to other customers.

        The CPUC supports the methodology proposed by the OCC that any proposed or

final rule should:

        1.     Prohibit the use of transmission credits, rate-based recovery,
               or regional cost allocation mechanisms for interstate
               transmission facilities built primarily to serve large private
               loads;
        2.     Require verification that interconnection-driven network
               upgrade investments associated with large load
               interconnections are necessary for system reliability and/or
               deliverability of electricity to the general public before any
               costs are shifted to consumers other than large loads; and
        3.     Ensure that transmission cost recovery aligns with current
               cost causation and cost allocation principles… 62
        The CPUC believes that transparency and standardized criteria for cost allocation

is a prerequisite for fair and accurate cost causation analysis. As stated by SEIA,

“[w]ithout clear methodologies, there is a risk that costs will be allocated inconsistently

or that one class of interconnection customer (load or generation) will be unfairly

disadvantaged. The Commission should therefore require transmission providers to

develop transparent, standardized criteria for determining cost responsibility in cases




62
  OCC Comments at 2. See also Illinois Commerce Commission v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476 (7th Cir.
2009) (ICC I).


589841566                                      20
 where both large load interconnections and generation projects contribute to the same

transmission constraints.” 63

          E.      Standard Definition of the Parameters of Inputs into
                  Methodology
          From the CPUC’s experience of working with large load energization in its Rule

30 proceeding, a standard definition of inputs into any methodology would be needed in

any final rule. For example, PG&E raised what constitutes a “network upgrade” and

asked several questions to that end, including inquiring (1) whether a network upgrade is

limited to upgrades to the existing transmission system or whether it also include a new

switchyard or substation needed to serve a large load or hybrid facility, and (2) whether

lines connecting a new large load or hybrid facility “network upgrades.” 64 Descriptive

technical definitions of common terms with examples would smooth out processes and

improve efficiency.

IV.       MEGAWATT THRESHOLD
          Based on the information received about the national data center market through

the Initial Comment phase, the CPUC shifts its positions on the MW threshold towards a

higher value and expands consideration of metrics for defining this large load customer

class.

          Initial Comments evidenced a broad swathe of positions on the issue of a

megawatt (“MW”) threshold to which a proposed rule would be applicable, with parties



63
     SEIA Initial Comments at 19.
64
     PG&E Opening Comments at 16.


589841566                                     21
 supporting threshold values as high as 300 MW and above. 65 The diversity of views on

the subject is indicative of regional differences, variation in rate structures, and weighs

strongly in favor of local determinations. The variation also suggests a moving target of

what constitutes a ‘typical’ data center customer. The Initial Comments indicate a

forming consensus, however, on the downsides of such a threshold being set too low.

          CPUC acknowledges OMS’s assertion that “many other states have approved or

are considering large load tariffs that all contemplate a range of 100-150 MW.” 66 Duke

Energy considers 100 MW to be the minimum threshold, advocating for a threshold of

300 MW or above. The CPUC’s experience with data centers in its region argues for the

higher-end of the spectrum. Per Industrial Customer Organizations, a 20 MW threshold

risks “captur[ing] a significant number of manufacturers and other industrial and

institutional entities.” 67 Further, EEI states, “[a] lower threshold may also produce

unintended detriments to economic development and reshoring activities.” 68

          Given the variation in regional market development and situations, MW metrics

alone may not be the defining feature of this type of load. The CPUC agrees with the

Ohio Office of Federal Energy Advocate (“Ohio FEA”) that data centers are a unique

customer class, and identifying them based on their exceptional characteristics is not

unduly discriminatory. 69 A better approach is states regionally determining the

V.      CONCLUSION
        The CPUC appreciates insights from other parties and the opportunity to provide

these Reply Comments for the Commission’s consideration. The CPUC encourages the

Commission to conduct this rulemaking in a way that embraces cooperative federalism,

acknowledges the jurisdictional authority of the states, and helps to support the efforts
